clue.text: Where are nails found? Everywhere

definitions.meaning: fingernails grow at the ends of the fingers, so they sit on a person's hands
an idiom for in every quarter, from all sides at once

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about where nails turn up, answered with a shrug: everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests nails in a hardware sense; the first reading is fingernails, found on all of a person's hands.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning from every side or by everyone, so it matches being found all over.

clue.text: French city I would end up in always, and hang in there

parts.note: Nevers is a city in central France, on the Loire

indicators.note: the reversed contraction is placed inside the word for always

parts.note: aye is an old and poetic word for always or ever

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'end up' turns this contraction so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: I'd is the contraction of 'I would'

explanation.surface: A traveller's encouragement: whatever French town you end up in, keep going and hang in there.
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue had dropped 'I', which the page prints. Nevers is a real French city, so 'French city' is not Paris or Nice; 'end up' turns the contraction in a down clue, giving DI.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exhortations to persist and refuse to give up in the face of difficulty.

clue.text: Lack ready ingredients for tea-time treat

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are treated as ingredients to be mixed into something new

explanation.surface: Someone without the makings for an afternoon cake has to go without.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ingredients' rearranges the letters of LACK READY. A lardy cake is a traditional English sweet bread made with lard, sugar and dried fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: This rich currant-studded bread is a classic English item served with afternoon tea.

clue.text: It protects locks out in the rain

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of the words that follow are disordered and rearranged

explanation.surface: Something that keeps one's hair dry when caught outdoors in a shower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' suggests door security, but here means hair. 'Out' rearranges THE RAIN; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine mesh cap is worn to hold hair in place and keep it tidy, guarding one's tresses.

clue.text: No officer with 1000 soldiers in position is crazy

parts.note: taken as written
NCO is a non-commissioned officer, such as a sergeant or corporal
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

indicators.note: the soldiers are placed inside the word for position

parts.note: a post is a position or job
men is a common word for soldiers, the ranks
taken as written

explanation.surface: A military report: a junior officer with a thousand troops in place has lost his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'position' as a military posting; it is simply a post. The answer is Latin for 'not of sound mind'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin legal phrase describes someone not in their right mind, that is insane.

clue.text: Official controlling race course, initially

definitions.meaning: the person who fires the gun or drops the flag to begin a race
the first course of a meal, served before the main dish

explanation.surface: Describes a racing official who runs things on the racecourse right from the off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race course' reads as one racecourse, but the comma splits it: the race official, and the first course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: The race official begins the race; the opening dish of a meal is the appetiser.

clue.text: Open a container

parts.note: a jar is a container, usually of glass

explanation.surface: An instruction to take the lid off a container.
explanation.definitionFit: A door left slightly open is said to be standing part-way unclosed.

clue.text: King who was responsible for Ambassadors?

definitions.meaning: several kings of England and Scotland bore this name
The Ambassadors is a novel by Henry ..., so its author was responsible for it

explanation.surface: Asks which monarch was in charge of sending out diplomatic envoys.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a king appointing diplomats; in fact 'Ambassadors' is the novel The Ambassadors, by Henry James.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a royal name and also the surname of the American novelist who wrote that book.

clue.text: Banter in speech lacking love

indicators.note: lacking tells us to take away the letter for love

parts.note: something done orally is done in speech, by word of mouth
love is zero in tennis scoring, so it gives the letter O

explanation.surface: Joking talk that has no affection in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking' removes O (love, nil in tennis) from ORALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: To rally someone is an old verb meaning to tease or chaff them good-humouredly.

clue.text: Dislike claim to Jerusalem

parts.note: to aver is to assert or claim
Sion, or Zion, is the hill of Jerusalem and a name for the city itself

explanation.surface: Someone objects to a nation's claim on the holy city.
explanation.walkthrough: SION is the older spelling of Zion, a biblical name for Jerusalem.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns describe a strong feeling of antipathy towards something.

clue.text: Horse, for example, requiring plate put back

indicators.note: put back tells us to read the word for plate in reverse order

parts.note: a lamina is a thin plate or layer of material

explanation.surface: A horse needing a plate, perhaps a horseshoe, refitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plate' suggests a horseshoe given the horse, but it is LAMINA, a thin layer.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse is one example of a creature, a living beast.

clue.text: Start to cram fabric in drawer

indicators.note: the start of the word cram is its opening letter

parts.note: rayon is a synthetic fabric made from cellulose

explanation.surface: Someone stuffing cloth into a chest of drawers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawer' reads as part of a chest, but means one who draws: a coloured stick for drawing.
explanation.definitionFit: A wax colouring stick is a tool used for drawing pictures, so it is a drawer.

clue.text: Not exactly honestly — though it could be

definitions.text: Not exactly honestly — though it could be

indicators.note: not exactly signals that the letters of the next word are given in an inexact, rearranged order

explanation.surface: A remark that something was done not quite above board, though it might have been.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not exactly' rearranges HONESTLY; the whole clue also defines the answer, since acting secretly is not honest, though the letters could be.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something secretly or furtively is not acting in an open and straightforward way.

clue.text: Scots magistrate and noble have drunk very old ports

parts.note: a lord is a nobleman

indicators.note: have says the rearranged ports hold the abbreviation for very old
drunk suggests the letters of ports stagger into a new order

parts.note: V is very and O is old, standard abbreviations

explanation.surface: A Scottish official and an aristocrat have been knocking back vintage port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' rearranges the ports to PROST, which 'have' wraps round the old pair. A Lord Provost is the civic head of a major Scottish city, like a lord mayor.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is held by the chief civic official of cities such as Edinburgh and Glasgow.

clue.text: Having no application, repeatedly, for children's nurse

indicators.note: repeatedly says the abbreviation is used twice in a row

parts.note: NA stands for not applicable, used on forms where a question has no application

explanation.surface: A nanny so idle that she has no use at all for the children.
explanation.walkthrough: NA (not applicable) is written twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Nana is an informal name for a nanny, as with the dog-nurse in Peter Pan.

clue.text: Want, ultimately, to reproduce top performance? You could do this

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of the word want

parts.note: to ape something is to copy or mimic it
a record is the best performance ever achieved

explanation.surface: Wanting to capture a star turn so it can be replayed.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the whole surface: to reproduce a top performance you could capture it on tape. 'To' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Capturing sound on magnetic tape lets a performance be played back later, which the surface invites.

clue.text: William sounds like a nutter, so to speak

indicators.note: sounds like says we need a word said the same way as the word for this nut player

parts.note: a conkerer is one who plays conkers, a game with horse chestnuts, so a nutter in the literal sense

explanation.surface: Someone says William's name sounds like he is a madman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nutter' (British slang for a crazy person) here means a conker player. Conkers is a British children's game of striking horse chestnuts on strings. 'So to speak' flags the playful reading. William I was William the Conqueror.
explanation.definitionFit: William, Duke of Normandy, who invaded England in 1066, is known by that title.

clue.text: Drew attention to strangely restive tot outside

indicators.note: outside puts the word for tot around the rearranged letters

parts.note: to tot up is to add

indicators.note: strangely says the letters of restive appear in an odd new order

explanation.surface: Someone noticed an oddly restless toddler out of doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strangely' gives VERTISE, which 'outside' places within the word for tot. 'Tot' suggests a small child, but here it means to sum up.
explanation.definitionFit: To publicise something is to draw public attention to it.

clue.text: Polishing stone found on Libyan coast

definitions.meaning: a porous rock, rottenstone, used as a polishing powder
the capital of Libya lies on its Mediterranean coast

explanation.surface: A polishing stone picked up on the North African shore.
explanation.definitionFit: The rock is named for the region where it was found; the city is Libya's coastal capital.

clue.text: Go-ahead police force pens a large number up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up says the whole assembly is read from bottom to top
pens means encloses, so the police abbreviation holds the large number

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of a British police force
many means a large number

explanation.surface: An enterprising police force locks up a lot of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' puts MANY in CID to make CIMANYD, which 'up' reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: Go-ahead as an adjective means energetic and enterprising, full of drive.

clue.text: Part in Italian opera? Certainly not

indicators.note: part in says a piece of the following words, running across them, is wanted

explanation.surface: A singer is asked to take a role in an Italian opera and refuses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' suggests a role to sing, but means a stretch of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a casual refusal, a colloquial no.

clue.text: Be first in the queue for a title

definitions.meaning: to head a line of people is to stand at the front of it
a heading over a newspaper story

explanation.surface: Being at the front of the line to win a championship.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper banner caption is the title over a story; 'head line' says lead a queue.

clue.text: Damp, nasty smell I had

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell
I'd is the contraction of 'I had'

explanation.surface: Someone remembers a dank, foul odour.
explanation.definitionFit: Muggy air is moist, heavy with water vapour.

clue.text: Obliquely make enquiries —— get conflicting directions

parts.note: to ask is to make enquiries
E and W, east and west, are opposite compass points

explanation.surface: Someone asking questions indirectly gets contradictory instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: Something set crooked or at a slant lies at an angle, not straight.

clue.text: Special cell, having run one in, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals that these letters may be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: A prisoner in a special cell has had one run in, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cell' suggests a prison; it is a nerve cell. 'Having' and 'in' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A nerve cell is a specialised cell that transmits signals.

clue.text: Ruler, mostly idle, attending a party

indicators.note: mostly says the word for idle loses its final letter

parts.note: to mike is old British slang meaning to idle or shirk
a do is a party or social event

explanation.surface: A lazy monarch spends most of his time going to parties.
explanation.walkthrough: MIKE, British slang for idling, loses its last letter. 'Attending' is a link joining it to A DO.
explanation.definitionFit: The title was used in English for the emperor of Japan.

clue.text: Tommy and other Tommies to fight soon

parts.note: Tommy is a diminutive of the name Tom
a Tommy is a British private soldier, and OR stands for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
a row is a quarrel or fight

explanation.surface: A soldier and his comrades are about to go into battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tommy', British slang for a private soldier, is used first as a name.
explanation.definitionFit: The following day is a time not far off, so it can stand for soon.

clue.text: Blue feathers

definitions.meaning: blue means sad or low in spirits
the soft fine feathers of young birds, used in pillows

explanation.surface: A description of a bird's blue plumage.
explanation.definitionFit: Sad and dejected means low in spirits; also the soft fluffy plumage of chicks.

clue.text: Try cuisine out, producing anxiety

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of the two words are thrown into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Trying a new kind of cooking makes someone nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' rearranges TRY CUISINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of confidence and worry are both forms of unease.
